Question: Is it ethically preferable to leave popcorn bags and soda cups at one's seat after a movie or to throw them out? If everyone disposed of their own trash, it would mean fewer jobs for people at the movie theater.
Answer: I’ve worked as an usher for two major multiplex cinemas. The cinemas I've worked with employed a cleaning crew who came in early at mornings to do the major clean up i.e. having the cinema spotless upon opening hours. Other than that it was the ushers were the ones given the sole responsibility to do the cleaning of all 8 cinemas and environs. After a movie finished we usually had 30 minutes to clear up all the trash and mess before the next showing. Besides that we also performed security duties, customer service relation duties and most of us were trained doing basic projection (‘threading a film’ as we called it) in case a projectionist took a sick day or quit. People were mostly neat and considerate when it came to their trash but there was certain to be the few outliers who left their seats in a disgusting state of scattered popcorn and nachos, spilt cheese and soda etc. We were not expected to be thorough with our clean up but at the same time no customer was to ever sit and feel popcorn under his/her butt, cheese on the arm rest and the stickiness of spilt soda at their feet. Mind you those cinemas were perennially understaffed. Nobody grows up dreaming of becoming the world's greatest usher. Rarely anyone below supervisory level stuck around in the cinema longer than a year. It was teenagers and college students on holiday who usually applied for the job. Many of them would leave after a month. When Big Budget Action Movie with Explosions Part 2 would make its grand summer premiere in the cinema, no patron would stay back to see what the place looked like when the light switched back on after hundreds of hyperactive children, angst riddled teenagers and fatigued parents had left. It would usually be an ugly sight. You and four other overworked and underpaid ushers had 30 minutes to clean up among the 8 cinemas before another batch of hundreds filed in. Keep in mind that you had to ensure little Johnny Mischiefmaker and his buddies didn't try to sneak into another movie after theirs had finished. Ushers were responsible for ensuring paying customers were the ones who sat on each seat. Failure to do this could result in money deducted in your salary. It wasn't uncommon to see one of my fellow workers running with a broom and scoop tucked under their armpits to tear tickets for people entering and then run to make certain another crowd of people from a finished movie exited the building and then run back to the first cinema to finish cleaning with 5 minutes to spare. All this for minimum wage and the ability to see a free movie once a week. Does that sound like a job someone would be desperate to hold on to? By throwing away your trash and keeping your seat relatively clean you are doing such people a great service. They are grateful to you even though they have no idea who you are most of the time. On the contrary if you believe that by being a sloppy bastard, spilling your food and drink and leaving all your trash on the seat and on the floor and have the audacity to claim that in doing so you are ensuring employment. No. You are ensuring the world that idiots still exist. You are making things worse for everyone around you. If everyone had your mentality cinemas would close down for good. So to the person who asked this question. When you walk the street at night and are unfortunate to get mugged, don't get angry with your mugger. With your logic if muggings no longer happened, it would mean fewer jobs for police. Edit: I never expected this answer to get so many views, upvotes and generate so much conversation. I truly appreciate. Please allow me to exploit the appreciation by including links to (kinda) humorous answers further describing my experience working as an usher.

Question: If your 3-year-old tells you there's a monster in their room, do you dismiss what they're seeing or feed into it asking them to describe what it is they saw?
Answer: My brother and I (13, 11) played cruel tricks on our sisters (5, 2) for our amusement. They were terrified of the character Venom from Spiderman. Being toddlers they thought that Venom was Spiderman. In the cartoon the Venom symbiote came from space. We told our sisters that ‘Spiderman’ is real and he actually lives on the moon. We were just joking around but we realised that this concept genuinely scared them. We upped the ante by telling them, whenever we were outdoors that we had to get back home, that it was getting dark and when the moon comes out Spiderman would see us and sling down to Earth and grab us. They would shudder and sometimes cry. One day my family was at the neighbourhood park. My brother and I had a pair of toy binoculars. A full moon was visible in the sky just before sunset. Our sisters started to grow discomforted. My brother looked into the binoculars up at the moon. ‘I can see him,’ he said, ‘There’s Spiderman. That's him.’ I took the binoculars. ‘Yeah,’ I said, ‘That’s Spiderman. He slinging all around the moon. He's as big as a truck. It looks like he's built a cage to fit two little girls. He's pointing at me. I think he's trying to tell us something.’ My brother, holding back laughter, snatched the binoculars, ‘Yeah he's ready to sling down to Earth, right here in this park. He's telling us don't move. Look for yourself and see.’ My brother attempted to give our youngest sister the toy binoculars but she burst into tears and ran to our mother who was chatting with a friend. My sister made such a hullabaloo that we had to go home. We told the older sister to be quiet, that it was all a joke. Our mother didn't take kindly to us pranking or scaring them. My mother couldn't make heads or tails out of our youngest sister's monster story. She just dismissed it as overactive imagination. In just a couple of months time they became all the wiser to our bullshit and we could no longer scare them so easily. In regards to the above question, I believe that there is some sort of logic and reasoning behind some of the fantastic stories children tell of monsters hiding under the bed or Spiderman slinging about on the moon. All parents should do some sort of investigation into these claims. Their fear is coming from a real place and many times the ‘monsters’ do exist, in my case it was two pesky, bored little boys looking for laughs.

Question: What small detail from a movie do you love?
Answer: So many to choose from in this movie. I’ll go with the more obvious. In So I Married an Axe Murderer (1993) Mike Myers plays the protagonist Charlie. He's a San Francisco native, the son of fiercely patriotic Scottish immigrants, particularly his father (also played by Mike Myers). When he brings his girlfriend Harriet to visit them, he's a bit embarrassed by their rustic simplicity, particularly that of his well intentioned but obnoxious, loud-mouthed father and retires to the bathroom. If you pay close attention you'll notice on the wall of the bathroom door is a dart board on which a photo of Queen Elizabeth is condescendingly taped on, demonstrating the stereotypical Scottish baby boomer/older generation hatred for the English. Also the scene where he is surprised to discover his enigmatic girlfriend Harriet speaks fluent Russian: Harriet: So what? Bright women intimidate you? Charlie (in a sinister voice): No. No. Not at all. But it's a shame I'm going to have to destroy you. Seems like just random dialogue but it's actually a tongue in cheek Cold War spy reference. Right after that Charlie puts on an Eastern European accent and starts dancing ballet. This is not random. This is reference to defected Cold War era Russian ballet dancers such as Baryshnikov and Nureyev. All of this in keeping with the ‘discovering your mysterious partner can speak Russian’ running joke. The movie is crammed full these little details of cultural ‘niche’ humor ranging from European stereotypes, San Francisco bohemians and hipsters, police work misconceptions, Alcatraz prison tours, butchers, fearmongering, aviation, absurdity of the media etc that one can only notice after repeated viewings. One of the many reasons why the movie has grown in cult status over the years. Edit: To all who are arguing in the comments that the photo on the bathroom door is Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother and not Queen Elizabeth (her daughter) and that it’s impossible for a Scottish person to hate the Queen Mother because she was Scottish herself. I appreciate the information but can we just get on with it. The point of the joke is the Scottish hatred of the English (represented by its royalty) so let’s not quibble too much and just appreciate the scene for what it is.

Question: What is your favorite quote from a movie critic?
Answer: Leonard Maltin has always been my favorite movie critic. I've learned more English adjectives from his reviews moreso than my entire school tenure. I love his terse conviction, his ability to convey his point without smugness and his economical use of words. This economy is the reason why he has an entry in the Guinness Book of Records. He will probably keep this record for all time. Guinness record for shortest review ever given to a motion picture: Isn't It Romantic (1948) Leonard Maltin's review: No. Nobody slays like the OG Leonard Maltin. Here are, as honorable mentions, a few excerpts from his famous review slays: ... It’s hard to think of a movie with more strident, obnoxious characters, or a script that makes so little sense from scene to scene. Three appealing stars are hung out to dry in this seriocomedy… …Title describes your inevitable state if you waste just two minutes watching this woeful attempt to revive screwball slapstick… No laughs whatsoever in this Clerks/Office Space slapstick wannabe, and the performances are awful. Shot in New Mexico; too bad they didn't bury it there… Is Sinise an alien spy impersonating a scientist married to Stowe in 2079? The movie’s distributor apparently didn’t think anyone cared enough to find out, because this malnourished Philip K. Dick adaptation sat on the shelf for more than a year. Most interesting features are the neat home appliances in the early scenes, which include a voice-activated wall-screen TV that shuts off on command. You should be so lucky when watching this movie at home. Idiotic action film boasts what may be the worst movie title ever coined…Only devotees of cars exploding into fireballs will find any value here Seagal is an undercover FBI agent who arrives as an inmate at a prison on the same day a team of crooks—get this—break into the joint, to get a condemned man to tell them where there’s a hidden stash of gold bars. To call this bad is an understatement . . . even by Seagal standards.

Question: Why do conservatives believe that poverty-stricken people are just freeloading off of welfare programs?
Answer: I am a conservative who came from a poverty stricken family who freeloaded off of welfare programs. Growing up my mother raised my brother and I as a single mother with no help from friends or family whilst working endless hours in various minimum wage jobs and taking up residence with whomever kind souls with give us cheap/free lodging. Well, that’s probably how she described it to our welfare officer. The reality was that she was not a single mother, we had a stepfather who worked in skilled positions in the construction industry. He was not dependable but calling her a single mother would've been a stretch. She did not suffer from ‘no help.’ We got monthly financial assistance from relatives on both sides of the family. She did work endless hours in various minimum wage jobs but she never stuck around long as she could’ve afford to quit when she got fed up. We used to beg lodgings with friends and relatives but that was a long time ago, in the 80s before she was allocated state housing. Now I’m sure all of this makes my mother look really bad, like a complete freeloader, but the reality is my mother is one of the better examples of welfare freeloading. If 65% of welfare programs saw results like that of my mother I would gladly be a staunch vocal supporter of it. However as an adult who worked in various distressed high schools I am always shocked how such is not the same with the overwhelming majority of students and parents operating through welfare programs: If I were to go on, this answer would be far too lengthy. Yes. There are shining examples of parents, like my mother, who use welfare for positive means and make a difference in their children's lives but I would say from my 15 years experience working in distressed schools that the overwhelming majority of welfare programs do little but foster bad habits and create an opportunistic and dependant mindset for poverty-minded families. I'm not arguing that welfare programs be removed completely. I argue that in my country welfare programs be tighter, stricter, far more transparent to the public, accountable and open to review and analysis by independent groups. It should stop being an expensive means to buy votes. In many ways it is a factor that is decaying the education system of Trinidad. Just my 2¢.

Question: What’s your favorite movie based on true events?
Answer: The Founder (2016) This is a movie I habitually return to watching. It's an inspiring movie but it's not a ‘feelgood’ movie per se. The movie tells the story of how a run of the mill salesman named Ray Kroc outmanoeuvred and outperformed the McDonald brothers and became owner of the McDonald's franchise/empire. I say it's not feelgood because, based on the film, Kroc was not by any account a ‘nice’ man when it came to business. He was a conniving opportunist but at the same time he was also unrelentingly persistent. His partners, the altruistic McDonald brothers derived a brilliant concept and product but had little interest in franchising and/or wealth. It is because of Kroc's persistence and willingness to take great risks that McDonald's is the success that it is today. If there is one concept the movie begs you to take away from it, regardless of your view of Ray Kroc, it is the value of persistence. Without giving away too much of the plot, this is what is inspiring about Kroc's efforts. There are so many profound scenes and quotes in this movie that it find it hard for anyone to not appreciate it for the sole merit that it generates a lot of thought, regardless of whether you don't like it or find Ray Kroc reprehensible. I think Michael Keaton gave his greatest performance and I was thoroughly disappointed that he was not nominated for an Academy Award. His persistence speech at the end of the film, I consider to be a classic in business motivation, trumping that of Jordan Belfort’s ‘sell me this pen’ in The Wolf of Wall Street and Alec Baldwin's ‘Always be closing’ scene in Glengarry Glen Ross. I beg to debate this opinion.

Question: What television shows started strong only to become unwatchable later?
Answer: Skins (2007 - 2013) The show was highly popular with millennials as it strove to give a realistic depiction of teenaged adults of that generation. The show, with its graphic portrayal of promiscuous sex and drug use among the majority of its main cast made it controversial at the time. Themes such as anorexia, poverty, depression, trauma, dysfunctional parenting etc were also touched on without succumbing to preaching or caricature. In essence the show was a comedy that subtly touched on some of the drama that went on in the personal lives of each of its characters. Generation 1 Without a doubt the first generation of Skins (Series 1 -2) is the true representation of the show. The first two seasons chronicles the lives of the above 9 teenagers. I enjoyed how no one was treated as the star of the show. Everyone had their positive traits as well as deep seated flaws but no one is given more screen time over the other or made into a token. The show focused on the youths as a group rather than as an hierarchy. The lifestyle may have been a tad exaggerated in its insistence that every character supposedly engaged in promiscuous sex and/or drug use. Besides that the show was an honest representation of teenaged millennials, written by an actual millennial, Jamie Brittain, who was 22 at the premier of the first season. The show launched the careers of actors Nicholas Hoult and Dev Patel who portrayed Tony and Anwar respectively. Generation 2 The second generation of Skins (Series 3–4) saw some changes. The comedic tone was increased as well as the amount of sex. The third season started off with an air of superficiality compared to the first generation but had a few well written moments and thoughtful episodes, particularly that of the trials and tribulations of teenaged Congolese immigrant Thomas. However the cast seemed all over the place and without developed characterization except that of cheap stereotypes (bully, geek, skater boy, drama queen, femme fatale etc.) Unlike Generation 1, this generation seemed to have an hierarchy among the cast as everything seemed to revolve around the characters Effy and Cook, who were, unsurprisingly, the most promiscuous and morally unscrupulous of the lot. Nearing the end of series 3 the show's writing started to wear thin. Shocks, drama and comedy were shoehorned in at every chance available. The show and its characters started losing their sense of direction and some of the themes that made them compelling characters in the beginning were abandoned in favour of sex and silliness. Some episodes were so ludicrous it became an effort to keep my eyes on the screen. The show seemed like a poor man’s imitation of itself. (So he's stealing a boat now…?) By series 4 it became painful to watch and I gave up. I have no intention to watch the third generation nor the American MTV remake. However the first generation of Skins remains a classic in my mind and a damned brilliant character study. It's hard for any writer to keep such a momentum going so you got to give the creators of the show credit for trying, even if they tried too hard in the end.

Question: Why is a bronze medal winner happier than a silver medal winner? What is counterfactual thinking?
Answer: Imagine Jimmy watching the lottery results live on television. 30 (Nice) 23 (Heyy!) 6 (Heyyyy!) 5 (Oh my God!) 8 (Oh my ****** God!) Jumps off couch And the final number… 33 (Nooooooooo. 33! Who the **** plays 33? It's 27. No. No.No.) Falls back onto the couch sobbing. Jimmy got 5 out of the 6 numbers correct. He is rewarded with one tenth of the grand cash prize. Jimmy is heartbroken. All his life he's waited for that moment. All his life he's played the National Lottery dreaming of the day. It was supposed to be today. He feels as though he wants to die. Better he had gotten zilch and saved himself this torment. Freddie is on his security shift. He hears on the radio that one person has won the grand prize. Some people have all the luck. He remembers he bought a ticket and checks to see if he scraped anything. He’s astonished to see that he got 4 out of 6 numbers correct. He got an entire year's salary through sheer luck. He is overjoyed. Far more overjoyed than Jimmy who got ten times his winnings. Moral of the story is that second place winners tend to feel overwhelming disappointment that they were so close to winning while third place winners tend to be happy that they at least got something.

Question: Is there a book so good that even today you have a hard time putting it down once you start reading it?
Answer: The last book that had me infatuated from the first page to the last is Trainspotting by Irvine Welsh. Every time someone tells me that they’ve seen the movie so they don’t need to read the book I get somewhat irritated. The movie is just a preview of an experience. The book is the experience. You know that famous ‘Choose Life’ quote at the beginning of the movie. A lot of people who saw the film remembers it because it sounded so cool to the backdrop of the song Lust for Life by Iggy Pop. The book expands on it to the point that it does more than just being a rock and roll metaphor . The ‘Choose life’ philosophy of a dishonest and at times pathetic junkie named Mark Renton makes sense to an almost frightening degree in his narration in the novel. The book is divided into several parts in a nonlinear order. Each major character narrates stories that highlight much of their varying personalities and how they are interconnected with the other characters. Some of the stories are of a bawdy, gross out and downright obscene humour, some are touching or insightful and a few are tragic. The novel touches on themes of alcoholism, racism, disenchanted youth, rock/punk and the growing threat of HIV/AIDS. It is more than just a story about junkies even though heroin does appear through most of the novel. Once I started deciphering the Scottish dialect I was immersed into a whole new world. Irvine Welsh has a gift for storytelling and does not judge his characters or tries to preach about right and wrong. The reader is left to make his/her own judgement. Many are fully aware of the ‘worst toilet in Scotland’ and ‘Spud and the bedsheets’ stories due to the film. The novel has these stories rendered far more effectively and uproariously funny due to its descriptive first person narration. One harrowing story that is unfortunately omitted from the film is the aptly titled Bad Blood. It centers around HIV diagnosed Davies who befriends a cynical, contemptuous man called Venters who is slowly dying of AIDS. They appear to have something in common which is revealed in its shocking finale. Trainspotting is the crème de la crème of dive bar gutter stories. It is the most beautiful and poetic piece of trash ever written in the 20th century. It is the type of sordid that makes one question the actual meaning behind the word sordid or if such a word has any meaning in reality. To read Trainspotting is to be taken outside, not just from one’s lifestyle but from one’s manner of thinking. As repulsed as I was by the characters and their choices it was impossible not to sympathize with them; a lot of what they did and said started to seem sensical in the mad world they created for themselves. It is this temporary indulgence into ‘insanity’ that made Trainspotting on of the most difficult books to put down.

Question: What Scorsese film would have been better if directed by Spielberg and vice versa?
Answer: Interesting question. In regards to Spielberg doing a Scorsese film, I know I may be in a minority but I never had much love for Scorsese's Gangs of New York (2002). I've never been able to sit through the entire film. In my honest opinion, just because the epoch the film is based on is an ugly period in history, it doesn’t mean that the film has to be inherently ugly. In the comparable and far superior Once Upon A Time in America (1984), Sergio Leone captures the pockets of childhood innocence and warm camaraderie in a truly poetic manner despite the inherent ugliness of the period documented. In Gangs of New York everywhere looked like a filthy trash heap. All the main characters were assholes. Everyone was somehow dressed in the most rattiest rags they could find. I think Scorsese was a little heavy handed in demonstrating the chaotic grittiness of the period. With the exception of Daniel Day Lewis the entire cast gave mediocre performances. The colours and camera work of the cinematography was glaring and unsettling and the whole revenge arc story didnt seem to have much of a point in the context it was used. In a nutshell the film was just a pointless, ugly film that just happened to have a measure of historical accuracy. Spielberg is the King of demonstrating the humanity that can be found in the absolute darkest periods of history. He does this without undermining historical accuracy or succumbing to fluffy melodrama. Of course the chief examples being Schindler's List and Saving Private Ryan. I think if Spielberg was given the job to direct Gangs of New York, the final product would've been a superior film with fleshed out, relatable characters, a better plot and overall a much more engaging experience for the senses. In regards to Scorsese doing a Spielberg film, I think the there is one film that was right up Scorsese’s alley that I think Spielberg’s did a disservice. Scorsese's eye for realism and portraying characters in their raw, unlikable form would've created a better product. No. It's not Munich (2005) It's Catch Me if You Can. The film was a the feelgood blockbuster movie of 2002. Frank Abagnale Jr was the antihero everyone couldn’t help but love, especially when portrayed by hearthtrob Leonardo DiCaprio. I enjoyed the movie when it premiered but it has aged poorly as of recently. Abagnale Jr was not just a scammer, it has been revealed that he is also a pathological liar. Much of the events described in his book are either grossly exaggerated or completely untrue. When you watch the film now you are treated to a self-indulgent, ego-stroking feast of fakery. I think Scorsese would've been a bit more skeptical towards the author's story and do the proper research into Abagnale Jr's life. The story would've been less attractive and a lot more cynical with moments of downright nastiness (very much in the vein of Raging Bull and The Wolf of Wall Street) but it might have been a compelling portrait of a fractured individual who thought more of himself than he actually was. It definitely wouldn't have the embarrassment that Catch Me if You Can suffers from today. So in conclusion, Spielberg and Scorsese should’ve simply traded director seats in the year 2002.

Question: What is the cringiest name you have seen/heard given to a child?
Answer: I worked in a school where there was a girl named Supreme Hurst. I asked her how she ended up with such a unique name and she said she hadn’t the faintest clue other than it was the name her dad chose. Out of curiosity I looked up her name to see if there was some kind of meaning behind it. I found out that there is an Oldsmobile car model with that very name. I would’ve loved to have known if it was by coincidence or intentional that her dad named her after such an unimpressive car. When I showed her the car she was quite disappointed it wasn’t a luxury vehicle. She explained that once she got married her name would change so it didn’t bother her that much. Some months later she got into a relationship with a boy named Stark Grimes. I kid you not. He’s not an aspiring rapper. That’s the name on his birth certificate. I was flabbergasted. The girl with the weirdest name I ever heard of was dating the boy with the weirdest name I ever heard of. I told her in jest that if they got married Supreme Grimes seemed far worse than Supreme Hurst. Stark wasn’t a bad chap. He was witty, well behaved and had a YouTube channel that had some pretty well produced Trinidad-oriented comedy. However the relationship didn’t last. Supreme Hurst and Stark Grimes went their separate ways after a few months of dating. Unfortunately I can’t find any of Supreme’s social media profiles. It’s been a decade since I heard from her. I’m assuming she got married and had that long awaited name change. I just hope for her sake she didn’t get married to a guy with the surname Dick.

Question: What was the worst meal that you ate out of politeness?
Answer: My friend invited me to a friend of her mother's who was having a BBQ lunch. Barbequed pork with fries and slaw was on the menu. For simplicity's sake we'll refer to the chef/mother's friend as Selma. Selma was in her 60s. Her grown children lived abroad and her husband had recently passed away. She lived alone in the deep countryside. They had a small farm when the husband was alive but Selma couldn't manage it by herself, in her old age and especially since she had been diagnosed with cancer. When my friend and I arrived there, her mother was there, already finished eating and chatting with Selma. Selma was quite pleasant. She was happy to have guests over. She was an aged woman living in such a remote location by herself and without a vehicle to access. She asked if we were ready to eat and we replied in the affirmative. Both my friend and her mother did not eat pork so I would be the only guest to have her BBQ pork that day. Selma assured me that I'd have the biggest serving of pork I ever had in my life since no one else was having it. I would also get a some to carry home as well. I was elated by the news. Selma however was not experienced in BBQ nor in preparing/cooking pork. As I was to discover later it was her last remaining pig that she had had killed just to get rid of it. The first thing I noticed was the amount of hairs that remained on some of the pieces of meat. I told myself I would simply avoid those pieces and tackle the hair free pieces. I managed to find a few and as I brought one towards my mouth I got a faint, gamey scent with a hint of excrement. I immediately brought the meat away from me and onto the plate. I had so much pork in front of me and Selma seemed so anxious to hear my praise. Selma, whose husband just died, whose children were far away, who lived in isolated poverty with the threat of a cancererous death looming around the corner was waiting for my compliment on her first BBQ pork dish. Upon close observation I could see that the pork was undercooked in several areas. I could hear Selma bragging that she didn't have a BBQ pit, she used her stove top with some wire mesh as a grill and a huge iron pot as a makeshift pit. I wish Selma would stop talking and go attend somewhere else so I could fling the pork into the bushes nearby. I searched for an unhairy, relatively well cooked piece among my pile that was devoid of the gamey, excrement scent. I found one and with great reluctance I bit into it for the sole purpose of trying to show proof that I ate some and give a positive compliment. It was ghastly. I ended up filling up on fries and slaw and afterwards explained that I was full. Selma packed the rest into a disposable container as well as a hefty serving ‘to carry to work.’ I thanked her and my friend decided she wanted to go see the circus that was taking place in a few hours. We left while her mom remained with Selma catching up on old times. Strangely enough my friend and I had a huge argument on the trip back that was unrelated to the meal. The argument ended with her demanding that I stop the vehicle as I watched her exit in the middle of nowehere, slamming the door. If I can recall well, the argument started because I asked her why didnt she want to wait for her mom so we could've given her a ride home/carry her to the circus with us. Her reply was that her mother could find a taxi and that she didn't want to go there in the first place. She didn't like the countryside, was irritated by her mother at the moment, found the place boring and was not fond of Selma ever since she was a child. Quite shocked that she could say/do something so mean and petty (especially given Selma's circumstances) I explained to her that it was selfish to be like that and the argument started there. We havent spoken since. I don't know what became of Selma as this was a decade ago but I hope she's doing alright.

Answer: My family went to see the premier of Fantastic Four (2005). Chris Evans played cocky, wisecracking Johnny Storm aka the Human Torch. He was the comic relief of the film. Question: What actor or actress got cast in a role that they normally wouldn't play and absolutely crushed it?
Answer: Everyone I know who saw Along Came Polly (2004) agrees that the standout comedic performance was… not Ben Stiller (The Ben Stiller Show, There's Something About Mary, Meet The Parents etc) nor Jennifer Aniston (Friends, Office Space, Bruce Almighty) nor Hank Azaria (The Simpsons, Futurama, Mystery Men) nor Debra Messing (Will and Grace, Ned and Stacey) The person who outperformed these four seasoned and well known comedians with decades of experience in film and television (and they were all excellent) was this guy. Phillip Seymour Hoffman At that point in his career Hoffman did not have the level of acclaim as he does now. He was mostly known for his eccentric supporting roles in mostly dramatic films such as Boogie Nights, The Talented Mr. Ripley, Happiness and The Big Lebowski. Just a year after starring in this zany comedy he played the role of Truman Capote in the the film Capote (2005), won the Oscar for Best Actor and from then on his status soared with him being called the greatest actor of his generation. It helped that his role was that of washed up actor Sandy Lyle who believes himself to be of the highest pedigree (despite never having a single role since a hit comedy in the 80s). Hoffman nails it with his character’s sometimes pompous, sometimes laidback mannerisms. He makes it seem effortless in that unique, low-key Phillip Seymour Hoffman style of his It's a pity that he died in 2014, at the prime of his professional career. He was finally being truly recognized for his talent and given leading roles. In my honest opinion, his performance in Doubt (2008) is without a doubt his greatest performance. I'm of the view he even outstaged Meryl Streep in their scenes together. I would've loved to see him take on more comedic roles. I think that he put his heart and soul into his performances and added his own subtle nuances to his characters. Even if you are like critics and don't think much of Along Came Polly, it's hard to hate Hoffman's unforgettable performance as Sandy Lyle.

Question: Why would I kill a mugger in self-defense? Are my valuables worth more than their life?
Answer: I’ve been mugged four times. Two of these muggings were violent. In these muggings I had my face punched relentlessly. I had a beer bottle smashed on my head, requiring stitches. I had a gun pointed at my face. I got my pants and underwear torn open and had to walk to the police station afterwards with my junk in my hands. In both muggings I got laughed at by the muggers. I’ll never forget the moment when one of the muggers looked at me sitting defeated on the curb, robbed, bleeding and beaten. I’ll never forget how in the silence that followed he looked me in the eyes and growled ‘That’s how it is.’ In that situation I’m certain that same mugger would’ve killed me if needed. I felt a deep cynical hatred in him; that beating me to a pulp satisfied some inner rage he compartmentalized towards society. No. It wasn’t just about the money for them. They felt the world owed them something that they themselves couldn’t fathom what. What is it that I had that was so valuable to these muggers? In total I lost around $300 TT (43US), a cheap cell phone and wallet with my identification cards which would’ve been no value to them. Someone who so callously and casually engages in theft while inflicting violence upon his victims is someone who has agreed that they do not value your life nor theirs. Why must I pay special consideration to their lives while being beaten senselessly or having a knife or gun pointed at me? Does the small amount of money lost bother me? No. What bothers me is the reality that there are some people out there who saw me like garbage and inflicted a hateful beating while threatening my life, knowing fully well that the loot probably wasn’t worth it. My valuables may not be worth more than a human life but if in self defense I had fatally shot my armed and/or violent mugger, I would not be sending flowers to his family nor showing up at his funeral, nor would I suffer any sleepless nights over it. As the old folks in Trinidad love to say; how you make your bed is how you lie on it.

Question: My girlfriend is mad at me for "not standing up for her.” She accidentally spilled her drink on a girl in the club. The other girl threw her drink on my girlfriend and her boyfriend shoved me. I grabbed my girlfriend and we left. What should I do?
Answer: I love pub stories. I have one to share in a similar context. Years ago my friends from work and I would visit a bar that was pretty much a flashy looking dive bar. There was 6 of us. The biggest guy in the pack was Kurt who would always bring his wife (then girlfriend) with him. Curt is some specimen of human. If Dolph Lundgren discovered he had a secret Trinidadian half brother, I would gladly tell Dolph to come check out Curt. Curt is a bug dude. He’s so strong that once, three us at work in the warehouse wanted to play a prank on him. We wanted to restrain him on his forklift and bound him onto it with shrink wrap; keeping him there until somebody discovered him. The three of us combined could not subdue Curt and our prank failed. Curt has a great sense of humour when it comes to pranks but when it came to his wife's safety, all jokes ended there. So six us were in this bar taking turns shooting pool. Kurt and his wife were sitting on bar stools against the wall while the rest of us were around a pool table. Suddenly a sound of a beer bottle crashing onto the floor could be heard from the opposite pool table. A pudgy little manchild held his pool stick as though ready to fight someone. His drunken girlfriend released a cackling laugh and was making a poor attempt to subdue him. Apparently the pudgy guy was drunk and believed some guys outside the bar were throwing sweet words towards his woman. He broke his beer as a show of machismo towards the men outside and proceeded to hurl threats their direction Curt and his wife were laughing at something else at the moment. Pudgy guy’s eyes narrowed in on them believing them to be mocking him. He took his girlfriend's beer and hurtles it into the air where it lands and splashes beer upon them both when it smashes near their feet on the ground. Everything went silent. My friends and I at the pool table believed that this was going to be a brawl like no other. Pudgy guy had already provoked the men outside who seemed ready to thrash him and now Curt Lundgren was ready to give Pudgy a demonstration. However Curt is a smart individual. He recognized immediately what was going on and calculated the outcome. Three agitated men ready to fight outside the pub, one drunken idiot stirring up more trouble every second that passed and his girlfriend seeing the whole thing as a joke, broken glass everywhere. If Curt engaged in a fight things would get ugly and his wife could get seriously damaged. Instead Curt decides that we should leave. Without a word we headed to our vehicles and went home. Had Curt been alone he would given Pudgy what he deserved. However bar fights do not play off like they do in those 80s action movies. Everyone involved gets hurts and some even get scarred, maimed or killed. The bar has since closed down after the owner got killed in a drive by shooting last year.

Question: What should every foreigner know about your country in terms of food, tourist destinations, demography, best time to visit, and USP of your country?
Answer: Trinidad is actually two islands, Trinidad and Tobago. Trinidad is the oil and gas island. Tobago is the tourist island. We have the only ‘pitch lake’ in the entire world. We invented the steel drum/pan. Yes we did. Look it up. Trinidad had the most thriving KFC in the world at one point in time. Also Trinidad has more KFCs per capita than any country in the world. 59 restaurants in an area smaller than Delaware (which has only 13). In many ways we are very similar to Brazil. We once possessed the world’s hottest pepper, the Moruga Scorpion (we still like to believe it’s the world’s hottest). We put ketchup, mustard and pepper sauce on EVERY fast food. Do not open a fast food restaurant here without having copious amounts of these available to the general public. Don’t even get us started on garlic sauce. If you hate rice you will not last a month here. We make some of the finest rums in the world. Yet beer is more widely consumed. Marijuana is sort of legal. Just don’t get caught selling it. We are very liberal yet quite conservative at the same time. We don’t frown that much upon prostitution, once you’re not a transvestite prostitute. Then you might be asking for trouble.

Question: Do you believe in "white privilege"? Have you ever witnessed/experienced it?
Answer: If I could humbly present examples of ‘white privilege’ I've observed here in the Caribbean. This is my father's friend Z (on the right). He is a white Trinidadian who happens to be poor. The area around him is at his house. He lives in a shed in the mountains with no running water or electricity. No. He is not a hippie or a hermit. It is through circumstance that he lives in such conditions. He had a period of his life where he was addicted to drugs and lived on the streets. He has turned his life around and now seasonally plants tomatoes for the person whose land he lives on. I've hung out with Z several times. He has a humble, salt of the earth type mindset and humour and is greatly appreciative of the little things in life (a decent meal, a hammock, a glass of cold water etc). At no point in my life have I ever seen ‘white privilege’ directed his way and I don't expect to. Z doesn't have a refined way of speaking, his clothes are always rough and oversized and he carries with him the scent of cheap perfume. People here notice his skin for a few seconds and when he opens his mouth that's where his privilege ends. Z is an anomaly because he is ‘white’ (skin colour, physical features etc) and ‘not white’ at the same time (speech, clothing, mannerisms etc). If that makes any sense. This is T. She is another white Trinidadian. I befriended her on a trip to Dominica in 2011. She came from a stable family but she herself was not someone who lived in comfort let alone possessed any measure of wealth. However, unlike the above mentioned Z, she was brought up to learn and demonstrate a certain refined image and social graces. She dressed well, spoke articulate and carried about herself like a cultured lady of means despite being in the lower-middle class bracket. T demonstrated her ‘white privilege’ to me one evening. At a beach our hiking group visited there was a rather nice hotel. Feeling adventurous we climbed the stairs to the hotel and saw that it took us to a stately but empty dining area overlooking the beach. Afraid that we would be unceremoniously kicked out I was suggesting we head back down the stairs. However T wanted to show me something. She told me to sit at a table and be quiet. She sat opposite me pretending to browse a menu. Within a few minutes a waiter arrived. He questioned as to what we would like to have. T said that she hadn't decided yet. The waiter, not annoyed in the least, asked if we would like any complimentary refreshments. T asked if it was possible we could have sparkling wine as the refreshment. The waiter said that usually soda or water was the complimentary refreshment but he would see what he could do. He came afterwards with some glasses and a bottle of sparkling wine which he poured for us both. He left the bottle with us and said that he would be available whenever we were ready. We pretended to browse the menu while drinking the wine. I whispered to her that now we would have to buy something or the waiter would make a scene. She laughed at my statement and said that she always did this on every island she visited. Sometimes she was even given free entrées as well just for looking the part of a respectable white woman. After we drank we left without a word I partook for a moment in her white privilege: being offered free sparkling wine at a hotel and not being chased off after not buying anything. And finally, this gentleman here was a family member of mine. I say was because he passed away over 20 years ago. He is quite clearly a white male individual. My memory of him is limited but from the best I can recall he was a booming, boisterous and charismatic man who worked odd jobs and semi skilled labour driving around in a pick up truck looking for work. His white privilege was that for a brief period of his life he got a lot of temporary but decent paying jobs (pressure washing buildings, cleaning windows etc) at greater ease than colored people looking for such jobs. However it has been said that he became an addict and from then on his downfall became rapid: divorce, losing custody of his son and then rejection in his job/personal endeavours. He fell on serious hard times, suffered from crippling depression and was found dead in his cramped apartment (details of which I cannot divulge). None of the above three examples experienced any significant favourable treatment in their lives other than a few inconsequential perks every so often. A complimentary glass of sparkling wine and a job to clean someone's windows can hardly be called ‘white privilege.’ Privilege is what happens due to factors that usually involve wealth, status and beauty, and it occurs in all races in all countries. So in conclusion in Trinidad and the greater Caribbean, there is a large degree of ‘white perks’ but I'm yet to see any significant examples of ‘white privilege.’

Question: What’s your relationship with alcohol?
Answer: As a self-described connoisseur of fine liquor I have to honestly say that my relationship with alcohol has reached something of a close. In my mid to late 20s, when I started to drink habitually, one stiff drink used to give me a solid buzz/near drunkenness that lasted a couple hours. A 750ml bottle of rum, vodka, whisky or scotch with a chaser of choice could last me a month and change. However this frugality was because I had little alcohol tolerance and was prone to hangovers. Excessive drinking was not greatly desired unless I had friends over or something to celebrate. In my early to mid 30s, what I consider my peak age of drinking, two stiff drinks gave me a solid buzz and anything over that got me into the tipsy/drunken spectrum. This lasted about two hours at most and I had great tolerance. Hangovers ceased to exist for me, partially due to experience but mostly due to self discipline. However my urge to drink started growing and I started to feel come downs more strongly and frequently. Now I’m in my late 30s. It takes me three stiff drinks to get a solid buzz that lasts 30 minutes to an hour. After this my come down lasts practically the rest of the evening and lingers into the next day. The urges are so strong that sometimes the first place I'm drawn to in a grocery is the liquor section. A 750ml bottle wouldn't last me more than a week at the height of my urges. The funny thing about alcohol is that when I reach that peak whereby my buzz is at its strongest but I've not yet condescended into drunkenness, I feel as though I’ve manifested into my supreme self. It tricks me into thinking my mind operates deeper and much more efficiently under its influence. The day I found on my phone a ‘supreme self’ video recording I did of me slurring and rambling about deep, self discoveries through alcohol, it did me a favour and proved otherwise. I'm not a shitty person when I'm drunk. Nobody has a problem with me intoxicated. I've never become uncouth, aggressive or self destructive when I drink. I'm a shitty person during the come down. I become sullen, withdrawn and easily irritated. I lose sight of my goals and ambition and I tend to focus on all my disappointments in life which opens the floodgate to anxiety and depression. I've come to the stage where alcohol takes away a lot more than it gives. Yeah, the occasional beer or cocktail makes me feel relaxed, temporarily kicks out my fears and anxieties and can even give me a boost of confidence but now I’ve found myself at an odd stage in my life where my body is both desirous of alcohol and yet repelled by it. As such I've been weaning off of harder liquor and instead been having an occasional drink of my own homemade fruit wines when the urges come. My wines are admittedly less than stellar and with an alcohol percentage so low it makes Coors Light look like absinthe. However even though weaning from alcohol has stopped me from feeling like Alexander the Great for an hour or so, it sure beats feeling like Eeyore the Donkey for hours on end afterwards.

Question: Which moments, either good or bad, do you still remember from your childhood?
Answer: As an 8 year old my school was a quaint little building with a population of a little over 100 kids; kids of lesser means like myself. The school was raising funds by sending us out to collect money through raffle sheets. The price of a chance on the raffle was a quarter. The 1st prize was an Oster blender. I found it pathetic and embarassing back then. People would give usally give us a dollar when asked, not because they wanted the blender but because they felt sorry for us; a lower tier school at the side of a river full of kids of lesser means. Instead of going about asking people for a chance in the raffle I slowly filled my sheet using my own allowance. However when I submitted the money and the completed sheet my teacher simply took it and gave me another raffle sheet to get filled out. ‘But I already filled out my raffle sheet!’ I protested. ‘One raffle sheet for an entire month Elijah?’ she replied tartly, ‘Kenrick filled out over 20 sheets already. He did 5 in the last two days.’ She was wrong. Kenrick probably filled out over 40 sheets. Us boys knew, from his sudden increase in wealth, that he was pocketing a lot of the raffle money as his own. I wanted to say this but I knew I had no evidence and even if I did I doubt she would've cared. I took the sheet but mentally refused to go about after school, tugging on strangers’ clothes putting on a sad face, begging for a chance in my raffle like Kenrick. I also refused to use more of my personal allowance to fill the raffle sheet. At the end of the week the principal wanted to see me in his office. My classmates were shocked. Only serious offenders, ripe for suspension, were called into the principal’s office. I was known to be a good boy throughout. In the office the principal chastised me for not getting my second raffle filled out and how I brought in the least amount of raffles of all the students in school. (A lie, my best friend didn't submit any.) He also threatened that if I didn't get 5 raffle sheets filled out by next week I'll be kicked out of the school. Yes. He literally said those words. I left office trying to hold my tears and when I was home my mother queried as to why I was so sullen. I explained to her what had happened. To my utter surprise she started to laugh. I asked her why she found it funny, that soon we would have to be looking for a new school. She told me to relax and that tomorrow she was going to make a phone call to my school. At the end of school the following day my teacher quietly asked me to return the raffle sheet. At assembly the following morning it was announced that raffle sheets would be suspended until further notice. In fact for the rest of my time in that school they never reinstated raffle sheets again. Whatever my mother said to the principal on the phone was effective. Most of the students were happy for the news, except Kenrick of course. Thankfully raffle sheet fundraising have become a thing of the past in most of our local schools. I'd like to think that my mother had a part to play in schools being banned from encouraging children to solicit money from strangers.

Question: Which is the most misunderstood film of all time?
Answer: It shocks me to this day that people think Breakfast at Tiffany’s (1961) is a charming, feelgood rom-com. Even though the screenplay was sugar coated to heck, the source material is actually a character study of grooming, abuse and promiscuity and its impact on a young rural woman deliriously pretending to be something she isn’t. No one talks about the Truman Capote book because reading it is a sobering experience that takes away a lot of the shimmer from the hugely popular movie. Holly Golightly is a really messed up, poverty stricken girl from Texas with the birth name of Lula Mae. She ran away from home to an older man through which she was groomed and became his wife at the age of 14. She then ran away from him to New York under a false identity. Through manipulation, fraud and mafia related espionage she maintains a high end Brownstone apartment above her means. She courts several wealthy suitors by throwing lavish parties and intends to marry the richest of the lot. In the film and the book she shows symptoms of borderline personality and disassociative identity disorder. When things don't go her way financially she goes further into her fantasy of being a high society socialite by simply walking around in her best clothes and pretending to shop/hang out at Tiffany's or other famous luxury stores and locations . Audrey Hepburn is cute and charming. Holly Golightly is not. She is a warped individual that is prone to fits of anger, delusion and self destruction. She is pretentious and borderline narcissistic with the only ease of conscious being her flimsy belief that she will help her abject brother at some point in time. This delusion does not work out well for her. If the film had ended the way the novella ended it would have been a tragic, small town, wide eyed kid comes to New York in search of the American dream drama very much in the vein of the not so feelgood Midnight Cowboy (1969). The final scene with Holly and Paul finding her cat (named Cat) in the alley in the pouring rain is supposedly where the moral of the story comes in. It is the part of the film that transforms it from a softened character study into a full blown romantic comedy. It gives a moral that love can heal all as both Paul and Holly acknowledge their faults, subtly agree to change their ways and direct their love to one another. I have ambiguous feelings towards the ending but it is admittedly cute. However, I think any licensed psychologist would agree that Holly Golightly from the film Breakfast at Tiffany's is a movie that is a somber study of the neuroses and disorders a young female runaway from a broken home has to endure disguised as a sophisticated rom-com. Edit: Several commenters have been stating that they don't see why I refer to this as a misunderstood movie, that it deviated from the novel but as a film it is not misunderstood. Yes it is a misunderstood movie. Many people believe it is a simple love story about two good looking, fashionable young people falling in love in New York to the tune of Moon River. Generations of people believed that Holly Golightly was classy, an inspiration and an icon in lifestyle and fashion. Many girls of the era grew up wanting to be just like Holly Golightly without thoroughly understanding that she was a deeply flawed character with deep seated personality disorders. If this is not a misunderstood movie then the word misunderstood is ‘misunderstood.’

Question: Was “The Wolf” in Pulp Fiction the kind of associate everyone needs in their life?
Answer: From reading most of the answers here I wonder what kind of sugar-coated lives many of our Quora writers live. People like ‘The Wolf’ in Pulp Fiction not only exist, they thrive, they commit acts that can be seen as heinous, they commit acts that can be seen as impressive. They are morally ambiguous. They have their own code and many of them will not personally commit murder but they have a view that most of the murders they help make disappear probably had it coming. What makes ‘The Wolf’ any different from the average politician or a top shot criminal lawyer? Tarantino wrote The Wolf as a fast talking, no nonsense, somewhat charming character. In fact I would go as far as saying that Harvey Keitel was the comic relief. I’ve read one’s answer claiming that he was a monster. Really? There's Vincent and Jules who would kill man, woman or child without asking a question. There’s Marcellus who is nothing more than a vicious Kingpin. There’s Mia who sleeps with this vicious brute for her own benefit. There’s Butch who’d rather kill a fellow boxer than suffer an ego blow. There’s the low life thieves Pumpkin and Honey Bunny who rob small diners for a living. There’s the sadistic rapist Zed and his depraved accomplices. Even Quentin Tarantino’s character Jimmy is a real dirtbag who is willing to help hide a murder before his wife gets home. The Wolf seemed like Captain Kangaroo compared to these ‘monsters.’ In my honest opinion, if we lived in a perfect world I’d like to have nothing to do with a character like The Wolf. But sad to say we don’t live in a perfect world. I would never like to have to know someone like him personally but I do understand that sometimes shit gets dirty and he’s the man to clean stuff up. I doubt there exists a person with a net worth of $10 million and over who doesn’t have a phone contact for a character similar to The Wolf.

Question: Which character did you view totally differently as a child vs. as an adult?
Answer: Roy Neary - Close Encounters of the Third Kind If there is one character who deserves the award for biggest douchebag protagonist Richard Dreyfuss’ performance of Roy Neary wins that award by a wide margin. He's a blue collar, salt of the Earth electrician, an honest man with a loving wife and two kids. While driving home at night he has an encounter with UFOs and his life suddenly changes dramatically. Without giving away too much of the story I'll concentrate on his character. As a child I saw Roy Neary as a hero, a distressed and eccentric one but a hero nonetheless. He worked relentlessly to uncover a secret Government rendezvous between humans and aliens about to happen in his area. He overcame all obstacles set forward by the Government, the army, secret service and his own family leaving him to prove himself right; that aliens and UFOs did indeed exist and the Government was indeed staging a landmark meeting between man and intelligent extraterrestrial life forms. Roy takes it even a step further. In the final moments of the movie he offers himself to the aliens and boards their ship amidst dozens of alien children. We are then treated to a rousing score accompanied by the beautiful flashing lights of the mothership as it majestically floats off into the sky and the credits roll. It is a fantastic scene full of wonder and innocence that only the likes of Spielberg could deliver. The End That is how I saw the film as a child. As an adult it was a completely different experience. Roy Neary was this a-hole who could give two farts about his wife and kids and all his responsibilities in life. His family didn’t leave him because they were impatient with his alien obsession, in fact they were remarkably patient with his bullshit. He stopped working and stopped caring about anything that didn’t involve anything regarding secret Government cover ups and aliens. However when he begins thrashing the house to build a model Devil’s Tower mountain and becoming a threat to himself, his family and neighbours are they forced to evacuate the premises in a state of trauma. Some people theorize that Roy was under some sort of mind control by the aliens and his actions were not willfully done, that everything was planned and coordinated by the alien masterminds. I argue that Roy was just a big A-hole. Why would the aliens have Roy come close to sabotaging the secret meeting with his annoying shenanigans? Roy acts with little intelligence and self control throughout most of the movie. He's like a selfish, impetulant and irresponsible child that must be the first in line to get the latest Playstation in stores. He has an ‘Us and them’ mentality whereby if you weren't an actual UFO witness or some half-cracked alien conspiracy theorist he didn't care about what you said and law and order didn't exist. I think Roy is a big stain on a great movie. When you think about it, none of his actions benefited anyone. Jillian would've gotten back her son regardless if she went Devil's Tower or not and his discovery would amount to nothing because no one would believe him afterwards. He ruined his family all so he could see some cool alien stuff and weasel his way into the heart of a grieving single mom. His character is supposed to be redeemed by offering himself to the aliens. To me he is just this UFO geek that wanted to escape paying child support. Lacombe: Monsieur Neary. You can't go aboard zat space sheep. What about your madame and infants? Neary:……my work here is done.

Question: What movies can you watch all the time and never get tired of watching?
Answer: Without a doubt Dirty Rotten Scoundrels (1988) is the movie I’d take with me to a desert island. I don't think the movie gets a fraction of the praise it deserves. I think it's the highlight of the careers of both its leads Steve Martin and Michael Caine. I must've seen the movie over 20 times and still it is a delight to sit and watch for its entirety. What makes it endearing as compared to great movies that you only watch once is that it doesn't take itself too seriously. There is no moral or lesson to be learned here. Two dirtbags, one a petty hustler, the other a gentlemanly con artist, make their living by manipulating wealthy, slow witted women. They make a bet as to who would be first to con a simple but good natured soap heiress who just arrived in the village at the French Riviera. What makes this film so rewatchable is that, yes it is silly movie, but it is also a very well written, well executed and thoroughly refined silly movie. The location and cinematography is absolutely gorgeous. The score and soundtrack is a fitting blend of waltzy French classical and sophisti-pop. Mostly filmed on location at scenic locations along the French Riviera, the film is one of the most gorgeous movies I've ever seen. From the beginning Villefranche-Sur-Mer train station to the breathtaking Beaulieu-sur-mer to the lookout at Villa Hier at the end, the film is a feast for the eyes. Not to mention the performances. Both Caine and Martin give stellar performances from a remarkably clever script but Martin steals the show and makes the character Freddy Benson his own in a highly physical role the likes of which only Martin can accomplish. Props also to Glenne Headly who plays mutual target of the leads, demonstrating an innocent charm that wins over the hearts of the conmen and the audience. The film takes a not so pleasant topic and turns it into a rather good natured, comedy film. If it were remade today it would be chocked full of the gratuitous profanity, nudity and sex that is the hallmark of modern day ‘comedy.’ There's not a single F-bomb, nor a sex scene, nor a gratuitous flashing of breasts etc. Frank Oz uses no cheap gimmicks to entertain an audience and as such the film can be enjoyed by the entire family. Watching Dirty Rotten Scoundrels is such a pleasure that watching it feels like a little vacation rather than a movie. I watch it every year as a sort of ritual and I am yet to find another movie that is such a timeless delight.

Question: Did you ever do something that was insensitive, culturally, racially, or otherwise, and didn't realize it at the time, but do now?
Answer: I must've been around 6. My cousin P was a 14 year old girl. P used to help my mother with babysitting me when she took my brother and I and ran away from our unstable (at the time) father and home. We were given a temporary lodging at her brother T’s house and P was one of his many children. T was a notorious womanizer and allegedly had many children with various women all around the country. Most of the children he denied paternity and refused outright. Sadly a lot of them grew up homeless or in orphanages. P was one of the three ‘lucky’ ones that T decided to accept paternity and raise. She was always a friendly girl, charming and gifted with an amazing sense of humour. Her voice was almost exactly like Miss Piggy from The Muppets and it was a delight for my brother and I to hear her. However her father was not a role model parent and she grew up missing the majority of school. At 14 she couldn't read or write properly. My mother, through her own sheer ignorance, would go about telling other family members and friends how dunce P was. She didn't notice that I listened to her when she said these things. At one point I heard my mother telling someone that P was so dunce that her 6 year old son (me) knew how to read and write better. As a 6yo, I couldn't decipher right and wrong so seeing that my very own mother openly called P a dunce, I assumed that nothing was wrong with that. The day after when P was babysitting me, she asked me to read one of my story books for her. Full of pride I sat and read it with gusto. After I finished reading P complimented me profusely on my reading skills, asking me if I was the brightest boy in school and whatnot. I then told her something that pains me to this day ‘Mommy says I'm the brightest boy in class. Mommy says you're a dunce. I don't want to be a dunce like you.’ I cannot remember her reaction but I do remember P attempting to laugh it off. What did I do seeing her smiling and laughing the hurt away. I kept repeating that she's a dunce, making a song of it even. P sent me off to play. I'm pretty certain what I said in my naiveté devastated her. P forgave me and my mother in time and no mention was ever made about it. It was only when I grew into my teens did the gravity of the situation finally register. To make matters worse I found out later that P was a victim of sexual abuse from the man she called father at the time. It's something that haunts me to this day when I think of it. Thank God P was a strong person and overcame all those difficulties she faced in life.She still retains that good spirit she's always possessed.

Question: What's the biggest anticlimax in movie history?
Answer: Bird Box (2018) was throughly gripping. All the characters were well fleshed out and relatable and as ridiculous as the premise was (unseen, omnipresent entities that makes one commit suicide if seen) the suspense and horror was so effective it became the most streamed Netflix film at the time, mostly due to word of mouth. SPOILER ALERT But by God what a stupid ending. After so much trauma in the first half of the film, years later Sandra Bullock’s character Malorie and her children (one biological, one adopted) are rowing blindfolded down a dangerous river to find the people who sent her a transmission as to a safe location. After a nail biting odyssey down the river we are all expecting to be given answers when she finally arrives at this mysterious, resistance base. What are those creatures? Where did they come from? What do they want? Why do people kill themselves just by looking at them? What is the state of the world right now? Do the entities have a weakness, is it possible to fight back? Instead the movie does the most dirty tactic that a studio could possible do. Instead of providing the audience what they waited for and dedicated our energy and emotions toward (answers) the studio goes the cheap route and decides to end the film by answering nothing, leaving the film open to sequels and prequels. This is a trend I’ve noticed in a lot of modern horrors and thrillers. They just can't end the effing movie and give us the closure that we waited two hours for. Ranting aside, Malorie reaches the destination, a school for the blind and everyone assures her that everything will be ok in one of the most corniest and cliched endings ever conceived. It’s a pity Malorie didn’t wake up from a dream and see all the familiar faces around her while uttering ‘There’s no place like home.’ I would’ve much appreciated that ending than the actual ending of Bird Box.

Question: What’s the biggest thing people take for granted in your country?
Answer: Land Development and Planning. Trinidad and Tobago scores a D when it comes to how we treat our land, how we value our land and how we exploit all resources involved with land. Just looking out my window I can spot several major infringements of land use, town and country regulations and the law in general. This is an apartment complex recently built opposite me. It should not be there. Why? Because as indicated by the arrows it is built under major power lines and next to one of the transmission towers. The photograph doesn’t demonstrate it but it is also on land lower than the road, making it vulnerable to flooding (of which the area is infamous for). The owner also didn’t see the need to finish a proper road and drain, rather just have some slippery gravel and aggregate and a dirt ditch alongside it. Not to mention a tiny makeshift unsecured bin, hardly noticeable in the right corner, susceptible to animals and for garbage falling into the drain. This is someone looking to profit off of land through renting apartments. In fact several locations in this area has seen an increase in these poorly planned apartment complexes built on lands that are not developed and/or restricted towards such use e.g on or near water courses, under power lines, earmarked for future roads etc. (As per above photos it is the norm for apartments and sometimes even entire private/state developments to be made and sold/rented/leased with little to no proper land development involved.) I’m no Town and Country Planning expert but with my limited knowledge I see infringements everywhere I go. People do what they want and the Government throws a blind eye and vice versa. We have many sprawling communities that develop in short time with little concern to what they see as minor issues such as drainage, waste and garbage disposal, efficient road networks, efficient water distribution etc. These guerilla communities make a domino effect in such that communities further down the line suffer from the bottlenecks and problems brought forward by a complete disregard of central planning. It is not uncommon to see garbage piled on the side of the road because people have sprawling and meandering hamlets with tiny narrow roads that twist and turn on a drunken path to nowhere, unable to allow for services such as garbage collection and other utility trucks to enter. Most people in the country do not get a steady supply of water in the country because of the lack of regulations and the increased demand for water when several people illegally build communities in locations that have already met its quota for residences to have a proper daily supply. The domino effect is ugly. People who have long maintained their land and property are now surrounded by these hastily built shantytowns. With them come an increase in traffic, crime, disregard to basic civil laws and a likewise reduction in the services that most communities enjoy. It also cuts off the potential for further development. No one wants to open a bowling alley, a Holiday Inn or a drive through cinema in a location that reminds them of the Wild West. Unregulated and illegal settling allows for an increase in the amount of illegal quarrying and polluting which creates a disruption of natural watercourses. This combined with large settlements, built without any prior land development and town and country standards, making flooding more disastrous than ever before in history. I know every country in the world suffers with varying degrees the issues brought forward by poor planning and regulation. However I would safely say that whereas in developed countries it is an issue found in small pockets of the country, typically in sparsely populated rural areas. In Trinidad and Tobago it is widespread and found practically everywhere, urban and rural. The problem here is a complete disregard of addressing the issue. In the past this was an issue that was an understandable reaction to poverty. It stemmed mostly from the inability of the Government to provide the housing needs for those who couldn’t afford property. Now it’s become simply a bad habit fostered from rich to poor, contractor to state official, peasant farmer to CEO; everyone is just making themselves comfortable doing what they please and in the end everyone is paying for it.

Question: What screams "I'm educated, but not very bright"?
Answer: I bought an old car that needed some work some time back. I brought it over to a friend of the family who recently started a mechanic shop and I thought it would be a nice gesture to give him the job to look over the basic servicing the car needed. He was no ordinary junkyard mechanic. This guy was educated. He sought after practically every certificate that was available in automotive repair and technology. He would watch countless videos on the latest trends in the automotive industry and could engage you in long conversation as to what is the best model car and brand to invest in at the moment. His father was a highly venerated machinist and from that he learned how to give engine heads the perfect optimization for power\speed etc. All that was fine and grand but I just wanted the basic servicing for my old vehicle; check the oil, brakes, suspension, steering etc etc. On the day that he told me to collect the vehicle I came to his garage and saw him sprawled on the floor next to the disassembled wheels looking as though he just heard news the love of his life had died. I asked him what was wrong. He said that he couldn’t figure out exactly why the brake pads weren’t fitting in the caliper no matter how hard he tried. He said that he even broke the clips of two pads trying to force them in and had to buy new ones (to my expense of course). ‘I’ve never had a problem like this before. I don’t know what’s going on. This is insane.’ He said this as though he suffered a crushing defeat at Waterloo. Now I don’t know anything about cars myself and I’m just the ordinary layman who could jumpstart, change his own tire, fuses etc. If this guy who held so many certificates in auto mechanics couldn’t figure out what was wrong with this caliper then something was seriously wrong with this car. I felt very upset that I made such a bad purchase. I then took a look at the caliper in question and immediately I saw the problem. ‘Why don’t you take out the old brake pads in the caliper to make space for the new ones?’ The ‘huh’ look that appeared on his face I could never forget. He took out the old ones and slapped in the new without any issue or further delay. I was flabbergasted. I was wondering if it was a good idea to carry this vehicle to him in the first place. He was intelligent but apparently he wasn’t very bright. The answer to my question came when I tried starting the car but got nothing when I turned the key. I watched him as he panicked and wondered what was the problem this time. He did everything right to his knowledge. ‘Isn’t that my battery over there?’ I said pointing to what looked like my car battery in the corner. ‘Right, right’ he said, ‘The battery.’ The bugger charged $1500 for his labour even though afterwards I found out that he didn’t clamp the exhaust back up properly and it fell down while driving. I had to tie it back to the chassis with some binding wire that I was lucky to have in the trunk. I owe him $500. He’ll be waiting a very long time until he gets that money.
