Question: Which zombie apocalypse show/movie had the best zombie outbreak intro?
Answer: I know this may be an unpopular opinion but the 1990 remake of Night of the Living Dead by legendary makeup artist/actor/stunt man/director Tom Savini holds the crown for best zombie movie and intro. While I appreciate George A. Romero for introducing zombies into modern culture with the original Night of the Living Dead (1968), I can't help but say that the film has dated a bit. Despite the excellent script with political/racial undertones there are several aspects of the film that distract me from the movie. 1.The original Barbara (Judith O'Dea) was rather annoying with her helplessness and incessant high pitched screaming. 2.The zombies, for the most part, were not very convincing make up wise. 3. The low budget aspect of it gets overwhelming at times with the camera work, lighting and sometimes jarring music. The 1990 version, in my opinion removed all these flaws by creating a more reserved and tactful Barbara, greatly enhanced the zombie makeup, behaviourism and gore and was more consistent with it's brooding sense of dread and eerie atmosphere. Instead of a frantic camera going all over the place as in the original, the shots are mostly static and you the viewer are are put in place to observe these zombies who startlingly wander at the corner of the frame then towards you. This is very evident in the well known intro where Barbara and her immature brother encounter two odd men whilst visiting their mother's grave. Critics dismiss it because the controversial ending of the original was changed in which Ben was shot dead by the sheriff subtly as a sort of racist connotation. This film doesn't try to subtly address racism and politics but there is an underlying message of sexism that many critics failed to realize. Barbara is tough and intelligent in this version. However Ben and the rest of the males dismiss her because she is a woman and whilst they continue to bicker amongst themselves on the plan of action Barbara accurately determines that the zombies are so slow that they would be better off leaving the house armed and footing it to the nearest town. No one pays attention to her. They pay the ultimate price in the end. From the music to the acting to the intensity of friction between all the characters, (even the farmhouse and the cemetery looks more foreboding) this was a great improvement by all regards imho. But you be the judge.

Question: Does your country have an icon whom you believe is grossly overrated? Is there someone who is underrated that should replace him/her?
Answer: Trinidad is not known for its success in the world of literature but whenever the topic comes up, this guy is always mentioned. V.S. Naipaul (1932 — 2018) If you go to Ireland to ask an average bloke who they think is the greatest modern Irish writer your mind might probably presume they will say it's this guy. James Joyce (1882 — 1941) But it's far more likely this guy would be the answer. Brendan Behan (1923 — 1964) But who's that guy? He looks like a fool. Isn't Ulysses by Joyce considered the greatest modern novel of all time? Ulysses by Joyce is always mentioned in every greatest English language novels list. Who are the critics who normally create these lists? Well duh. The English. Joyce wasn't particularly admired by his fellow men during his lifetime. Constantly imposing self exile to Switzerland and France, he wrote high-brow, experimental novels that condescended and stereotyped Irish nationalists and appealed to the literary elites in Paris, London and New York. His funeral in Zürich, Switzerland was ignored by the Irish diplomats residing there and was attended only by the British Consul. The Irish government refused to repatriate his body Behan was almost the opposite. He was a staunch Irish Republican, an IRA member, an unapologetic alcoholic, was fluent and sometimes wrote in Irish. He was working-class witty, impulsive and had a larger that life attitude that led to his untimely death at age 41. He was the hard-drinking, self-destructive patriot that Joyce would mockingly caricature. In other words he definitely wasn't someone the English hierarchy at the time would think too fondly of. His funeral was then considered one of the biggest Irish funerals since Michael Collins. What does all this have to do with V.S. Naipaul? It's almost the exact same scenario in Trinidad literature. Naipaul was a writer of some talent who basically turned his back on his country, played monkey for the British by writing in some imitation Dickensian style about how backwards his home country was and in return was given citizenship, a slew of affirmative action awards and false praise. Having over ten years experience working in public libraries, I can say with confidence that the one of the best lanes to reshelf is the Fiction NAI - Naipaul section. The books there are always untouched. Anytime someone actually borrows a Naipaul book it is either a tourist or some eccentric literature snob looking for something to brag about. Otherwise the dateslips in his books are spotless clean of due date stamps. His early works portray Trinidadians as either cartoonish simpletons living in dirt huts or petty street scamps and beggars in the city and his later work reeks of cynical, self praise. His prose in my opinion is dull and many times hard to comprehend with his constant attempt at stretching out a sentence or finding a big, archaic word to replace small one. Here is a sample from his book The Mimic Men (1967) "Coconut trees and beach and the white of breakers seemed to meet at a point in the distance. It was not possible to see where coconut turned to mangrove and swampland. Here and there, interrupting the straight line of the beach, were the trunks of trees washed up by the sea. I set myself to walk to one tree, then to the other.” I almost fell asleep just copying and pasting that. Why the second unnecessary 'and’ in the first line? Why not say ' foaming waves’ instead of 'white of breakers?’ Who on Earth says 'I set myself to walk…?’ It sounds like the voiceover for another pseudo artsy Chanel advertisement. These types of pompous passages could be find throughout his ouvre. Naipaul is to many Trinidadians the classic sell out. His personality was not known to be a pleasant one. He proudly exclaimed his distaste for his country calling being born in Trinidad a mistake. After winning the Nobel Prize in 2001 he failed to recognize Trinidad in his press release. For his return trip to Trinidad he was asked to visit several schools and advise young aspiring writers. He requested to be paid and was irritable and condescending, basically telling impressionable young men and women that his novels were above their intelligence. He was a bastard in his personal life. He used his first English wife as a stepping stone as she fervently sought to get his work published in England. When he got his big break he got on his high horse and chased after women around the world, coming home to verbally and mentally abuse her, calling her sexually unattractive. He did not mourn for her when she died in 1995 as much as he mourned the death of his cat. To me he was nothing but a pretentious, overrated curmudgeon and variations of this sentiment is shared throughout the island. So who is underrated and should take his place? This dapper young fellow here is called Samuel Selvon (1923 —1994) He is very much the Brendan Behan of Trinidad in my honest opinion. Selvon wrote as a form of expression, not to kiss ass and self praise. He was proud of his roots and gave a thrilling, funny heartfelt and completely unbiased account of Caribbean 'Windrush’ emigration to England in the 1950s, complete in local dialect in his masterpiece The Lonely Londoners. He did not try to sound like Dickens while bashing his homeland and praising how great England is like Naipaul but his book made a great impact and is considered a modern classic. He died of respiratory failure while in the Piarco airport returning to Trinidad in 1994. It's almost as though he held back death until the moment he touched home soil. Question: Would Hollywood actor Brad Pitt have made it in old or classic Hollywood back in the day?
Answer: Very interesting question. For the sake of simplification let's just assume that by Classic Hollywood you mean the Hays Code era of Hollywood whereas sex, nudity, graphic violence, rape etc could not be demonstrated in Hollywood films. (1934 — 1968) 1930s — 1940s Hollywood Hollywood in the aftermath of the Great Depression and the outbreak of the Second World War. This is the age of the Go-Getter and although silent movies are now obsolete, it's exaggerative stage acting style is still rampant. Audiences of this era are favorable towards a certain type of male screen presence. Popular actors of the era are mostly an embodiment of what were considered desirable, manly traits. This is the era of Clark Gable, Cary Grant, Gary Cooper, James Stewart, Errol Flynn, John Wayne and Henry Fonda. The archetypal male film star was usually tall (over 6 feet), athletic, handsome, possessing a rich and resonant voice and possessing a certain self assured alpha male quality. The kind of man who would've made a great career as a top salesman or workforce motivator. The nation was wounded after two World Wars and these idealistic tropes were coveted by men and women alike. It was an age that was obsessively preoccupied with courage, persistence and survival. It was the era of sucking in your emotions and holding your chin high. Unless in possession of exemplary acting skills or song and dance expertise, actors who lacked several of these traits were relegated to minor supporting roles, comic relief roles, extras, stunt work or failed to make it in the film industry at all. Despite being ruggedly handsome, Brad Pitt would've had a hard time getting work in Hollywood during this era. He did not fit the height requirement, his voice would not be considered rich and animated and his brooding, sombre presence would've been a turn off for a national audience hungry for the next cocky, high shouldered, go-getting macho man. 1950s Hollywood The ideal aforementioned leading man is still prevalent with Charlton Heston, Gregory Peck, Burt Lancaster, and Rock Hudson maintaining the status quo. However standards are less rigid as actors like William Holden, Frank Sinatra, Kirk Douglas, Yul Brynner and Tony Curtis, who have the macho appeal but lack the height, are some of the top stars. A growing interest in brooding more sensitive type 'method' acting is gaining ground with the likes of James Dean, Marlon Brando and Paul Newman. Brad Pitt would've been better able to find work in such type roles but the competition would be fierce and only those with extensive stage experience and schooled in New York at the Actor's Studio would get top priority over some quiet, good looking guy from Missouri. 1960s Hollywood The growing counterculture revolution is finally making an impact on Hollywood. While the war scarred older generation is fading to make way for the Baby Boomers, the conservative values and ideal macho leading man is no longer as appealing for those hungry for emotional catharsis. The audience is yearning for a leading man who they could relate to, who shares their flaws and can demonstrate vulnerability. Even the more macho type actors are expected to demonstate weakness and more sensitivity. These would include Clint Eastwood, Sean Connery, Charles Bronson, Steve McQueen, Robert Redford, George Kennedy and Rod Steiger. Slurred speaking (Marlon Brando), meek voiced (Eastwood) overweight (Steiger) and short stature (Bronson) are traits no longer shunned by Hollywood elite. Brad Pitt would've found the greatest chance of obtaining prominent roles during this era. Who knows he might've even replaced Robert Redford in Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid.
